newsitem.title: USA: NYC FY 1997 surplus may top record - sources.
newsitem.headline: NYC FY 1997 surplus may top record - sources.

text.p: New York City's 1997 surplus might surpass the record of about $570 million, said city officials Monday, citing a variety of factors, from strong profits on Wall Street to better management.
"The only question is how big the surplus is going to be," said a city official, who declined to be named.

A spokeswoman for the Giuliani Administration declined to comment. Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who is scheduled to unveil the fiscal 1998 budget on May 8, forced agencies to make deep cuts in the early years of his Administration, and proposed $558 million of new reductions in a preliminary plan.

At least one city official remained cautious, pointing out New York City's fiscal year still had two months to go. "It's going to be large," he said, referring to this year's surplus, but added: "It's still moving."

New York City this spring has been fairly conservative in its revenue estimates, sticking with predictions that it would get an extra $181 million by the end of the 1997 fiscal year on June 30. However, several city offiicals, all of whom requested anonymity, said that the city had taken in about $150 million more than it forecast.
"We noticed that cash is substantially higher too," said another the city official. "There's no denying that we're better off."

New York City, which struggled during a sharp, local recesssion in the early 1990s, was expected to roll its big 1997 surplus into the next fiscal year, and partly use it to prepay expenses. The City Council, which forecast that the city would collect an extra $146 million of revenues this year, proposed salting away some of the funds in a Rainy Day Fund, so they could be used if the economy faltered. But setting up such a new fund would require approval from both Giuliani and Albany lawmakers.

In 1992 and in 1985, New York City's surpluses totaled about $570 million, a city official said, adding he could not immediately determine which year had the bigger windfall. He noted that the figures were not adjusted for inflation.

While Wall Street's powerhouse financial firms earned more than $11 billion in calender year 1996, continued strong earnings from this sector were not the sole factor producing the big windfall, as city officials also cited less foot-dragging from Albany in paying its bills.
"It's the fact that the state has been paying us on time," said one. He noted that the Board of Education's monthly statement showed it had around a $75 million surplus.

The Giuliani Administration, which has been faulted for not doing enough to rescue New York City's students from over-crowded, crumbling schools, was not planning on taking the money away from the agency, another city official said.
Others warned against counting all of the Board of Education's surplus, saying it in part hinged on getting funds from Albany.

The city's coffers also appeared to be getting a boost from a program designed to speed property tax payments that were late. "We think what we're seeing is a one-time, spin-up in property taxes," said one of the city officials, explaining that while around 90 percent of these taxes are paid on time, the lagging 10 percent seemed to be coming in earlier than anticipated.

Additionally, the Giuliani Administration has postponned wage increases for unionized employees until the later years of their contracts. For example, city workers who are represented by District 37, a coalition of unions, did not get raises until mid-April--the first pay hike in two years.
